observations.quote: How, and with what Vertue, Physick worketh upon Mans body and cureth his Diseases
observations.what: CHAP. IV. How, and with what Vertue, Physick worketh upon Mans body and cureth his Diseases
observations.note: The chapter is headed and numbered as one subject: how, and by what vertue, physick works on the body and cures.

observations.quote: THat which Physitians commonly dispute and contend for
observations.what: That which Physitians commonly dispute and contend for
observations.note: One question is set apart as the common dispute of physitians: cure by contraries or by like. Quote corrected to the text's spelling THat.

observations.name: Hippocrates
observations.quote: according to Hippocrates his Maxim, that Contraryes are to be cured with CONTRARYES
observations.note: The maxim that contraries are cured with contraries is given to Hippocrates.

observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.quote: or Like with LIKE, according to Paracelsus
observations.note: The opposing maxim, like with like, is given to Paracelsus; the paragraph frames the two as what physitians dispute.

observations.name: lib. de flatibus
observations.quote: In lib. de flatibus.
observations.note: The margin note names a writing beside the sentence giving the two maxims; its mark stands just before the naming of Hippocrates his Maxim.

observations.quote: these Maxims may be both received in the Anatomy of Nature, though they seem thwart one the other
observations.note: The author holds that both maxims can be accepted; their disagreement is only seeming.

observations.quote: many attaine not the Mind of Phylosophers, which to them seems to be at variance, because they cannot understand how to reconcile them by a seasonable and sutable interpretation
observations.note: Stated: the philosophers' meaning is missed by many, and their seeming variance is removed by a suitable interpretation; their words are not to be taken as they first stand.

observations.quote: Physick is nothing else but an opposition of those things that are desired, to wit, a refreshing of the strength and Balsom, and a removing of superfluityes or impurities that cause diseases
observations.note: The text says what Physick is: refreshing strength and Balsom, and removing the superfluities or impurities that cause diseases.

observations.name: Hippocrates
observations.quote: hunger is to to be cured with meat, thirst with drink, fulnesse with evacuation, inanition with reflection, labour with rest, idlenesse with labour
observations.note: Examples of cure by contraries given as the saying of Hippocrates, with the general rule that contraries cure contraries.

observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.quote: Paracelsus therefore doth not find fault with Hippocrates
observations.note: The author reports that Paracelsus accepts Hippocrates' contraries in this sense.

observations.name: Galen
observations.quote: who applyed that Contrariety of Hippocrates chiefly to those bare and naked qualityes which Hippocrates utterly disclaimed
observations.note: Galen's application of Hippocrates' contrariety to bare qualities is reported in order to reject it; Paracelsus is said to be poynt blanck against him.

observations.name: Galen
observations.quote: referred the first and principall Idaea's of Cures to Refrigerations, Calefactions, Humectations, Exsiccations
observations.note: Galen's view, called an unhappy mistake: cures referred to cooling, heating, moistening, drying. The sentence says he; the nearest name before it is Galen.

observations.quote: The onely and alone NATURES of Physicall medicines, as hath been said
observations.note: The words as hath been said point back to an earlier place; the lines given do not show which.

observations.quote: those Hippocraticall vertues are they which doe the cures, the Physitian is but the minister or servant
observations.note: The natures of medicines, also called Hippocraticall vertues, do the cures; the physitian only serves.

observations.quote: this very selfe same Nature, which is our Life and Balsom, or balsomicall Mummy, that preserveth the body from all corruption
observations.note: Nature is said to be our Life and Balsom, or balsomicall Mummy, which keeps the body from corruption.

observations.quote: the Saline moysture, that is, of the inferiour Balsom springing up in the inferiour from the superiour
observations.note: The Saline moysture is explained as the inferiour Balsom, springing up in the inferiour from the superiour.

observations.quote: sometimes worketh wonders, when the Physitians to their great disgrace and shame of their Profession could doe no good
observations.note: Nature sometimes works wonders where physitians could do nothing and had left the patient to their prognostics.

observations.quote: is its own proper Physitian in Mans body, who asketh nothing of the outward Physitian but Instauration
observations.note: Our own Nature is the proper physitian in the body; it asks of the outward physitian only Instauration.

observations.quote: Instauration, or as tis commonly called, fortification applyed to the diseased part by a most pure medicine when the like Nature is not at hand
observations.note: Instauration is given its common name, fortification, applied to the diseased part by a most pure medicine when the like Nature is not at hand.

observations.quote: the Medicinall Balsom like a coadjutour or privy counsellour assisteth the Vitall or Radicall and Naturall Balsom because of the simpathy and common agreement between them
observations.note: Two Balsoms: the Medicinall one from outside helps the Vitall, Radicall and Naturall one within, by the simpathy between them.

observations.quote: which being restored it is of it selfe able as an inward and unknown Antidote to chase all its enemies out of its Monarchy by the onely power of the Vitall facultyes
observations.note: Once the natural strength is restored it drives out its enemies by its own power; it is figured as an inward and unknown Antidote ruling a Monarchy.

observations.quote: Nature cureth with like things.
observations.note: The margin note sums the paragraph as cure by like things.

observations.quote: To go about to cure a disease with contrary qualities, is to raise and stir up intrinsick commotions to the utter overthrow of Nature
observations.note: Cure by contrary qualities stirs up inward commotion and overthrows a Nature already weakened.

observations.quote: where there is no true action and passion, there can follow no true Naturall effect
observations.note: A further reason against contraries: they do not willingly entertain each other, work on or suffer from each other, so no true natural effect follows.

observations.quote: medicines should not be contrary to the grieved part, but very agreeable to it, and have the same Externall Nature (because of the Harmony between the great and little world) as the place affected hath the Inward
observations.note: The medicine should agree with the affected part and have outwardly the Nature the part has inwardly; the reason given is the Harmony of the great and little world.

observations.quote: Man is therefore called a Microcosm or little world, because the whole world preserveth, nourisheth and cureth him
observations.note: The text says why man is called Microcosm or little world.

observations.quote: When the fruits of the Earth, Aire, Water and Fire of the Microcosm are sick, they must be restored by fruits like themselves of the Macrocosm
observations.note: The sick fruits of the four elements in man are restored by like fruits of the great world.

observations.quote: Nature strengthened and assisted by its own Nature doth more forcibly drive out all its enemyes, seeing every Nature is Naturally the best preserver of it selfe
observations.note: Nature helped by its own Nature drives out its enemies more strongly; each Nature best preserves itself.

observations.name: Galen
observations.quote: it alone being the genuine Physitian of all diseases, as Galen witnesseth in his 13 Book of Method
observations.note: Galen, in his 13 Book of Method, is called as witness that Nature alone is the physitian of all diseases, though CH4.2 sets Paracelsus against him.

observations.quote: It is the First Mover of every cure, without whose strength and vigour all Physick is in vaine and to no purpose
observations.note: Nature is named the First Mover of every cure; without it all Physick is in vain.

observations.quote: Nature continued in its Temperature is in it selfe medicinable, and it selfe healeth its own infirmities by the innate Mummy
observations.note: Nature kept in its Temperature heals its own infirmities by the innate Mummy; without the inward Nature diseases prove mortal.

observations.quote: every thing by a kind of naturall instinct desireth to be perfected and preserved
observations.note: Given as well known: every thing desires its own preservation and abhors its destruction.

observations.quote: those that are wounded perceive a presentaneous succour from Nature as of one hastening to helpe
observations.note: Daily experience of wounds is brought as proof that Nature hastens to heal and does not rest till the wound is cured.

observations.quote: they are not much mistaken if they have not respect to the qulaityes, but the vertues of a contrary Nature
observations.note: The saying of unnamed some, that contraries cure contraries, is allowed if it is meant of vertues of a contrary Nature, not of qualities.

observations.quote: there are as many crosse and hurtfull vertues to nature as there be good and healthfull for it
observations.note: Two kinds of vertues are set against each other: hurtful ones that destroy Nature and good ones that preserve it and drive the others out.

observations.quote: contrary qualityes, are not rooted out by contrary quallityes, but rather are irritated and provoked to strife by each other
observations.note: Contrary qualities do not remove each other but provoke strife, by which Nature is weakened.

observations.quote: Nature is not a quality but a vertue
observations.note: The text says what Nature is: a vertue, not a quality; it is therefore helped by vertues.

observations.quote: Nature her selfe (who is the Internall Mummy or inward Balsom)
observations.note: Nature is said in a bracket to be the Internall Mummy or inward Balsom; she, not the physitian, expels disease.

observations.quote: when her own inward strength fayleth shee is to be supplyed with outward helpe by her servant the Physitian
observations.note: The physitian is Nature's servant and supplies outward help when her inward strength fails.

observations.quote: sometimes it may be the best medicine not to use any medicine at all but to leave the ooperation to the sole Archaeus or Art of Nature
observations.note: The best medicine is sometimes none, the work being left to Nature alone.

observations.quote: the sole Archaeus or Art of Nature
observations.note: Archaeus is paired by or with Art of Nature, as another name for the same thing.

observations.quote: The Inward Physitian doth the work, when the Naturall Physitian faileth.
observations.note: The margin sets an Inward Physitian against a Naturall Physitian that fails; the paragraph calls Nature the inward one and the physitian her servant; the lines given do not say who the note's Naturall Physitian is.

observations.quote: it is not by the coldnesse of Opium, but but by the Specifick venemous vertue of the Opium which hath a greater degree of poyson then the occult venomous power of that Pestilence
observations.note: Opium preserves in a pestilence by its specific venomous vertue, a stronger poison than the occult venomous power of the pestilence, not by its coldness.

observations.quote: Thus Nature destroyeth one poyson by another, it subdueth a weak evill by a stronger
observations.note: Nature fights with hurtful as well as healthful weapons.

observations.quote: As winter doth not destroy summer, nor summer winter, but one gives place to the other, so one quality doth not destroy another
observations.note: Qualities do not destroy one another; the seasons are the comparison.

observations.quote: without vertue the quallity is dead and wholly accidentall
observations.note: A quality without vertue is dead and accidental and gives no life or substance, which a medicine must give.

observations.quote: Roots of diseases in the body of Man are neither hot nor cold
observations.note: The roots of diseases are neither hot nor cold; disease is only said to be hot or cold.

observations.quote: those Accidents and Excrements are but the signes of the disease, and not the disease it selfe
observations.note: Heat, cold and excrements are signs of the disease, not the disease.

observations.quote: do not spring out of the matter of the body, or out of the four Humours, but from the Nature of the Seed or Astra's and Invisible mechanick Spirits of the Three principles
observations.note: The worst diseases come not from the body's matter or the four Humours but from the Seed or Astra's and invisible mechanick Spirits of the Three principles.

observations.quote: which Spirits also build their outward house and habitation with shells
observations.note: The same invisible Spirits are said to build their own outward house with shells; a figure for the visible part of a disease.

observations.quote: These Forgers and Invisible Astra's of diseases were not knowne to the Ancients.
observations.note: The author says these Forgers and invisible Astra's of diseases were unknown to the Ancients. Kind corrected from concealment: the text speaks of what the Ancients did not know, not of hiding.

observations.quote: Physick is a Spirit (not a body) which the Magician or wise man only can discerne
observations.note: Physick is a Spirit, not a body, which only the Magician or wise man can discern: a thing open to some only.

observations.quote: the body or Earth of Simples is to be cast away
observations.note: A step of work: the body, also called Earth, of the Simples is thrown away.

observations.quote: the vertue Heaven or Astrum of it only to be taken
observations.note: The other half of the step: only the vertue, also called Heaven or Astrum, of the Simple is kept.

observations.quote: it is necessary that the life should worke upon the life, and the Spirit upon the Spirit by sepration of the impure body, as the intangible Sun Melteth Snow and causeth it to vanish away
observations.note: Life must work on life and Spirit on Spirit by separating the impure body; the likeness given is the sun melting snow.

observations.quote: Such is the Nature of all Secrets that they worke without the matter and body because the diseases also are not bodyes
observations.note: Secrets work without matter and body, because diseases are not bodies.

observations.quote: This is the true and lively Anatomy.
observations.note: What has just been said (life on life, Spirit on Spirit, without the body) is named the true and lively Anatomy.

observations.quote: This Mechanick and Forger of diseases is to be subdued and destroyed in his Roote and originall
observations.note: The maker of the disease is to be destroyed in its root; N189 beside it names Paracelsus.

observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.quote: Paracelsus in the Tincture of medicines.
observations.note: The margin note names Paracelsus and a writing beside the sentence on destroying the Forger of diseases in his root.

observations.quote: the Mechanick Forger or principle of a Pear's generation hath his habitation in the Roote, not in the branch
observations.note: A likeness from trees: the principle of generation lives in the root, so a tree is destroyed in the seed, not the branch.

observations.quote: the grasse which groweth of its own accord is hindred from growing, not by evultion but corruption of the Earth
observations.note: A second likeness: grass is stopped not by pulling it up but by corrupting the earth; given for cure at the root.

observations.name: great Surgery
observations.quote: See the first Tract of the second book of great Surgery
observations.note: The margin note sends the reader to a writing, great Surgery; it does not name its author.

observations.quote: Degrees and complexions are not considered in diseases.
observations.note: The margin states that degrees and complexions do not count in diseases.

observations.quote: when the Centre, Root, and Seed of diseases are pluckt up and removed the worke is done
observations.note: The cure is done when the centre, root and seed of the disease are removed.

observations.quote: That Physitian which cureth by complexion is like him that would extinguish the hurtless flame and let alone the fire in the coals
observations.note: Cure by complexion is likened to putting out the harmless flame and leaving the fire in the coals.

observations.quote: in doing the cure the Roote of the seed which containeth the vertues is to be taken in hand
observations.note: What springs from the seed is not the disease; the cure takes in hand the root of the seed, which holds the vertues.

observations.name: his Book of ancient Physick
observations.quote: In his Book of ancient Physick.
observations.note: The margin note names a writing beside the sentence on the root of the seed; it says only his and does not show whose book it is.

observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.quote: When Paracelsus saith that like preserve their like, and are destroyed by their contraryes
observations.note: A saying given to Paracelsus: like preserve their like and are destroyed by their contraries; the author then says what it does not mean.

observations.quote: he doth not meane the first nor second qualityes which he alwayes calleth Recollaceous and invalid ones, but the substance
observations.note: Stated: like and contrary in Paracelsus' saying are meant not of the first or second qualities, which he calls Recollaceous and invalid, but of the substance. The gap-only note N192 stands at this point.

observations.quote: at least the Cherionic, Hippocraticall powers and vertues
observations.note: The substance meant is narrowed to the Cherionic, Hippocraticall powers and vertues; the word Cherionic is not explained here.

observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.quote: first Tract of the second part of his great Chyrurgye, and in other places
observations.note: The reading of Paracelsus' saying is supported by the 18. Chap of the first Tract of the second part of his great Chyrurgye, and other places not named. A gap stands in the words before the quote.

observations.quote: Like things are said to be the Remedies of diseases because they are of the same Anatomy of Nature, and because they have the like Signatures, Qualities and Roots
observations.note: The text says in what sense like things are called remedies.

observations.quote: because they have the like Signatures, Qualities and Roots
observations.note: Likeness in Qualities is a ground of cure here, while CH4.4 and the same paragraph deny that qualities cure and say Paracelsus does not mean qualities.

observations.quote: Contraryes cure because they piece up the defects and wants, because they appease the spirits and consentaneous impurities with a friendly saturity, and because they attempt resolutions, consumptions and tacit ablations
observations.note: The text says in what sense contraries cure: they fill up defects, appease the spirits and impurities, and attempt resolutions, consumptions and tacit ablations.

observations.quote: Diseases are cured by applying that which is proper for them.
observations.note: The margin note states cure by what is proper to the disease.

observations.quote: That Like are to be preferved with their Like is thus to be understood, viz. that the Salt, Sulphur and Mercury of the Microcosm is preserved by the Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury of the Macrocosm analogically agreeing together
observations.note: Stated: the text says how like with like is to be understood: the Salt, Sulphur and Mercury of man are preserved by those of the great world, which agree analogically.

observations.quote: in the Microcosm there are various Sulphurs (one of the head, another of the heart, &c.) and various Mercuryes and Salts
observations.note: Each of the three is many in man, by part of the body, answered by a matching variety in herbs and minerals.

observations.quote: The ministry of Fire discovereth their agreement, operation, and difference
observations.note: Fire is the means of finding the agreement, working and difference of these substances; the text does not say here how it is used.

observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.quote: he distributeth all materiall diseases according to those three substances of which our bodies are composed, and according to the excrementitious superfluities arising from meat and drink
observations.note: A division of diseases given to an unnamed he; Paracelsus is the person named just before (CH4.6) and in N194, so the name is an inference.

observations.quote: he called them Sulphurean diseases, such are all Inflamations and Feavers
observations.note: Diseases from kindled and flaming Sulphur are named Sulphurean; all inflammations and fevers are of this kind.

observations.quote: as Sulphur may be deprest or heightned four wayes, viz. by the four Elements
observations.note: Sulphur can be lowered or raised in four ways, by the four Elements.

observations.quote: Those that proceed from moysture he Mercuriall.
observations.note: Diseases that come from moisture are named Mercuriall.

observations.quote: Mercury may three manner of wayes be exalted above the Naturall degree
observations.note: Three ways are numbered: by heat of an accidental digestive vertue, by heat of exercise and labour, by heat from the Astra's.

observations.quote: By the heat of digestion it is distild, and so causeth all sorts of Apoplexies
observations.note: Mercury distild by the heat of digestion causes apoplexies; a word of work is used of what happens in the body.

observations.quote: by the heat of Excercise it is sublimed
observations.note: Mercury sublimed by the heat of exercise; madness and frenzy follow.

observations.quote: by the heat of the stars it is precipitated, and then causeth the Gout in hands and feet &c. from eating and drinking those things that have too much Tattar in them
observations.note: Mercury precipitated by the heat of the stars causes gout; food and drink with too much Tattar is named with it.

observations.quote: those diseases that are bred of Salt, he calleh Saline and Nitrons
observations.note: Diseases bred of Salt are named Saline and Nitrons, as what he calls them.

observations.quote: Salt destroyeth health 4 wayes, by Resolution, Calcination, (loosing its liquid and humid Temperament) Reverbertion. Alcalization
observations.note: Four ways are numbered and named: Resolution, Calcination, Reverbertion, Alcalization.

observations.quote: all which are diseases arising from the Salt dissolved
observations.note: Ulcers, scabs, tetters, ringworms, itch and the like are put down to dissolved Salt.

observations.quote: Surfetting and gluttony which destroy the digestion is the cause of the Salts destruction
observations.note: Causes of the Salt's destruction: surfeit and gluttony; excess and luxury dissolve it; the stars thrust it out of its degree.

observations.quote: Which Salt may be changed and turned into all sorts of Salts, and such as is the Transmutation such also is the disease
observations.note: The kind of disease follows the change the Salt undergoes.

observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.quote: He saith therefore that the Sulphur kindled in mans body is to be quenched with the Sulphur of the great world, which harmonically agreeth with the other
observations.note: A saying given to an unnamed He: kindled Sulphur in man is quenched with the agreeing Sulphur of the great world. Paracelsus is an inference from CH4.6 and N194.

observations.quote: he that considereth to what end he spake it will find that such a remedy will be contrary to the disease
observations.note: Stated: the saying is to be read by its purpose; so read, the remedy is contrary to the disease.

observations.quote: his meaning is, that appropriate Sulphur should be used
observations.note: Stated: for a feverish fire that is universal and flows from the heart, the Sulphur meant is an appropriate Sulphur from herbs and minerals.

observations.quote: as Sulphur of Vitriol, Niter, common Salt, and such like
observations.what: Sulphur of Vitriol, Niter, common Salt, and such like
observations.note: Examples of the appropriate Sulphurs are named.

observations.quote: there are many to be had in Natures Garden, and the Family of Hearbs and Mineralls
observations.note: Herbs and minerals are called Natures Garden and a Family.

observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.quote: he saith that Ulcers proceeding from Salts must be cured by Salts
observations.note: A second saying of the same unnamed he: ulcers from Salts are cured by Salts. The name is an inference, supported by N194 beside this paragraph.

observations.quote: if we observe his drift, such Salts are contrary to that which was the cause of the disease, and quite opposite to the disease it selfe
observations.note: Stated: read by his drift, the curing Salts are contrary to the cause of the disease and to the disease, though they bear the same name.

observations.quote: they are incarnative and consolidative, as Frankencense, Mastick, Myrrhe, Aloes
observations.note: The curing Salts are named by what they do and by examples, gums and resins.

observations.quote: sometime he calls that Salt whatever it be that will melt, and may be resolved into a watry moysture, and then dryed and hardened by Fire, such are the thickned sap and juyces of Trees and Hearbs
observations.note: The text says what Salt sometimes means in his usage: anything that melts, dissolves to a watery moisture and is dried and hardened by fire; the word is not always meant plainly.

observations.quote: All Terresterity is the Salt of Paracelsus.
observations.note: The margin note says what the Salt of Paracelsus is: all Terresterity.

observations.quote: Cumfry cureth the corrosion of Salt.
observations.note: The margin pairs remedies with faults of the three: Cumfry with the corrosion of Salt, a word with a gap in it with the dissolution of Sulphur, Gold with Mercury.

observations.quote: Gold thickneth the too much sublimation of Mercury.
observations.note: Gold is said to thicken Mercury that is sublimed too much.

observations.quote: Our Nature cureth all diseases when he impediments are taken away
observations.note: Our Nature cures once impediments, the causes of diseases, are taken away; our part is to assist Nature against them.

observations.quote: As there are Three from which all Physick proceedeth, Mercury, Sulphur, Salt; so likewise there are three sorts of diseases, Mercuriall, Sulphurean, Saline
observations.what: Three from which all Physick proceedeth
observations.note: The three from which all Physick proceeds and the three sorts of disease are numbered, named and set side by side.

observations.quote: All Ulcers are cured by incarnating Mercury; All mattery gluish sores by Salt; All Inflamations by Sulphur
observations.note: Three rules of cure are given, one for each of the three.

observations.quote: All Ulcers are cured by incarnating Mercury
observations.note: Here all ulcers are cured by Mercury; in CH4.9 ulcers from Salts must be cured by Salts, and CH4.8 lists ulcers among diseases from dissolved Salt. The lines given do not reconcile the two.

observations.quote: This needs no Reasons to confirme it.
observations.note: The author gives the three rules without proof and says none is needed.

observations.quote: Medicament though they be contrary to the disease, yet they must of necessity be altogether courteous to Nature
observations.note: A medicine may be contrary to the disease but must be friendly to Nature.

observations.quote: if she sinck or miscary the Physitian can doe no good
observations.note: If Nature fails the physitian can do nothing.

observations.quote: if she abide and be kept safe and sound she worketh incredible wonders
observations.note: Nature kept safe works wonders; the two stories that follow are brought in as instances.

observations.quote: A stupendious and true Story.
observations.note: The margin sets the account that follows apart as a story and vouches for it as true.

observations.quote: As was seen in the New City at Prague, Anno 1602. in a certaine rustick or countryman of Bohemia, whose name was Mathew, about 36 years of age
observations.what: As was seen in the New City at Prague, Anno 1602.
observations.note: A case fixed by place, year, the man's name and age is given as an instance of Nature's wonders.

observations.quote: he swallowed it so far that it went down quite into his stomack, so that he could by no means get it up againe
observations.note: The knife he used to hide in his throat went down into his stomach and could not be got up.

observations.quote: by application of drawing Plaisters made of the Load-stone and other things, the poynt of the knife began to force its passage, by a naturall impulse, near the mouth of the stomack
observations.note: Drawing plaisters of Load-stone and other things not named were applied, and the knife's point began to come through near the mouth of the stomach.

observations.quote: it was prosperously performed by Florianis Mathis of Brandeburge chiefe Surgion of the Kingdome and City, upon thursday after Whitsunday at seven a clock in the morning
observations.note: The knife was cut out by a named surgeon at a stated day and hour, at the man's own request.

observations.quote: The knife was nine fingers breadth transverse in length, his stomack had changed the colour of it just as if it had laine so long in the fire
observations.note: The knife's length is given, and that the stomach had changed its colour as fire would.

observations.quote: it is now laid up among the Emperors rarityes, and hath been shewed as an incredible Miracle to many both in Court and City
observations.note: The knife is said to be kept among the Emperors rarityes and shown to many.

observations.name: Mathew
observations.quote: the Country man could eat and drinke and sleepe, as he told me, without any manner of paine or trouble
observations.note: The countryman's own report of his recovery, given to the author in person.

observations.name: Physitians Aphorismes
observations.quote: contrary to the determinate assertion of Physitians Aphorismes
observations.note: The recovery is set against what the Physitians Aphorismes assert; the lines given do not quote the assertion.

observations.quote: in the year 1606. at Prague a certaine Silesian to get mony did in the presence of many swallow six and forty white flints which he gathered at banck side, weighing almost three Physick pounds
observations.note: A second account, fixed by year and place: a Silesian swallowed forty-six white flints before many people.

observations.quote: all of them being almost four of my handfulls
observations.note: The author measures the flints by his own handfuls.

observations.quote: without impairing his health, he went up and down getting his living for many years together, &c.
observations.note: The man lived on unharmed for many years; the account breaks off with &c.

dropped.reason: Not borne out: CH4.6 speaks of the grieved part, CH4.11 of the disease; the text keeps the two apart, so they do not conflict.

voices.quote: that Contraryes are to be cured with CONTRARYES
that hunger is to to be cured with meat
voices.basis: Hippocrates named, for saying, that ...; runs to that Contraries cure Contraryes

voices.quote: who applyed that Contrariety of Hippocrates
voices.basis: Galen named; his view reported to reject it, called an unhappy mistake; runs to with their companions

voices.quote: it alone being the genuine Physitian of all diseases
voices.basis: as Galen witnesseth in his 13 Book of Method

voices.quote: that contraryes are to be cured by Contraryes
voices.basis: whereas some say; the author then allows it on a condition

voices.quote: This Mechanick and Forger of diseases
voices.basis: margin note N189 at the end of this sentence names Paracelsus and his Tincture of medicines; where his words begin the text does not show

voices.quote: as the whole Tree cannot be destroyd in the branch
voices.basis: notes N190 and N191 name writings (great Surgery, his Book of ancient Physick) beside these lines without naming whose words they are; runs to is to be taken in hand

voices.quote: like preserve their like, and are destroyed by their contraryes

voices.basis: which he alwayes calleth; he is Paracelsus, named in the sentence
verbs of naming he called, he Mercuriall; he is unnamed, the nearest name is Paracelsus (end of CH4.6, his great Chyrurgye); runs to the end of CH4.7

voices.quote: Mercury may three manner of wayes be exalted
voices.basis: no verb of saying; continues the account of the unnamed he between his namings; runs to too much Tattar in them

voices.quote: those diseases that are bred of Salt, he calleh Saline and Nitrons
voices.basis: he calleh; the same unnamed he
no verb of saying; continues the account of Salt diseases; runs to such also is the disease

voices.quote: He saith therefore that the Sulphur kindled in mans body
voices.basis: He saith; the same unnamed he; runs to agreeth with the other, where the author's reading begins

voices.quote: he saith that Ulcers proceeding from Salts must be cured by Salts
voices.basis: he saith; margin note N194 to this paragraph speaks of the Salt of Paracelsus

voices.quote: the Country man could eat and drinke and sleepe
voices.basis: as he told me; the countryman named Mathew earlier in the paragraph
